newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian reforms hold the key to general election.
newsitem.headline: Romanian reforms hold the key to general election.

text.p: The sluggish state of Romania's free-market reforms, far behind most other east European states seven years after the demise of communism, is the issue likely to decide the outcome of Sunday's general election.
But analysts say no matter who wins in the election, the new leader will have to speed up restructuring of industry and agriculture and make Romania more energy-efficient.

"Romania must build a strategy for industry and proper financing for farmers to get healthy growth," analyst Ilie Serbanescu said. "We cannot ignore that our energy bill is now oversized compared with the export capacity."

President Ion Iliescu, in power since the 1989 overthrow of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and the leader in opinion polls, portrays himself as a guarantor of stability. He points to improvements in inflation and economic growth in the past year.
His ruling Party of Social Democracy, forecast to be lying in second place for parliamentary elections, also on Sunday, says it can prevent the sort of collapse now gripping Bulgaria.

Iliescu's two main rivals, academic Emil Constantinescu and former Prime Minister Petre Roman, say the president has shunned the fast-track reforms used to build up Poland and Hungary. They accuse him of plunging millions of Romanians, already poor under communism, into abject poverty.
The International Monetary Fund has also objected to the pace of reforms and withheld recent loan installments.

Gross domestic product in the Balkan country remains below the 1989 level. And though purchasing power is officially down only 30 percent, average monthly wages of less than $100 are one-third of the level in countries embracing faster reforms.

The leu currency has sunk from 21 to the dollar under the communists to 4,300 offered by retail traders, who ignore government attempts to maintain an artificial rate 25 percent higher than on the interbank market.

Payment arrears remain a major problem, with the backlog almost at the same level as Romania's money supply. Inflation, cut to 27.8 percent last year, is on the rise again with the year-on-year rate hitting 45 percent last month.
Farm output, which helped achieve 1995 growth of 6.9 percent, has also slumped again in a largely rural country. And inventories of goods no one seems to want total 60 percent of monthly output.
Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu's government has also kept the subsidies tap open for inefficient state industry and allowed wages to rise, putting the budget under severe pressure.
The deficit of 1.9 trillion lei ($563 million) in the first eight months is forecast to balloon to 4.2 trillion by the end of 1996.
"The main problem is the lack of budgetary contraints for the industrial sector," said Andrew Kenningham, senior economist with Merill Lynch International.
But there are bright spots.
Industrial output over the first nine months of the year rose 8.7 percent and the trade deficit shrank to $588.5 million, half of the figure a year ago.

And Romania, which cleared nearly $10 billion in foreign debts under Ceausescu's extreme austerity plans, has made a comeback on private debt markets after decades of absence, raising about $1.4 billion in medium-term loans.
It also won credit ratings from major agencies, although its place is below investment grade and the levels awarded to Hungary and Poland.
Iliescu denies that the gap separating Romania from Eastern Europe's relatively successful economies has grown.

"I don't think the gap is increasing between us and other countries in central Europe," he told Reuters last week. But he added: "We do have a handicap to be overcome in the coming years." ($1=3375 Lei)
